claim: Malaria caused an estimated 241 million cases and 627,000 deaths in 2020, mostly by Plasmodium falciparum.
source: Malaria, a disease caused by the single-celled eukaryotic parasite Plasmodium, caused an estimated 241 million cases and 627,000 deaths in 2020, mostly by the species Plasmodium falciparum (P. falciparum; WHO Report 2021).
evidence: Cited from WHO Report 2021

claim: The WHO made its first recommendation for widespread use of a malaria vaccine, RTS,S, in 2021.
source: In 2021, the World Health Organization (WHO) made its first recommendation for widespread use of a malaria vaccine, RTS,S.
evidence: Statement of fact about WHO recommendation timing

claim: The efficacy of RTS,S is only 30–40% and protection wanes in a few months despite a four-dose regimen.
source: While this is an encouraging step, there is nevertheless need for improvement as the efficacy of RTS,S is only 30–40% and protection wanes in a few months despite a four-dose regimen (Clinical Trials Partnership, 2015; Olotu et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Clinical Trials Partnership, 2015 and Olotu et al., 2016

claim: Natural protection against malaria requires multiple exposures and wanes upon cessation of exposure.
source: Natural protection against malaria, particularly protection from uncomplicated malaria and ability to control parasitemia, requires multiple exposures and wanes upon cessation of exposure (Doolan et al., 2009).
evidence: Cited from Doolan et al., 2009

claim: Naturally acquired immunity to malaria develops gradually with age and increasing cumulative exposure to P. falciparum in endemic settings.
source: This naturally acquired immunity develops gradually with age and increasing cumulative exposure to P. falciparum in endemic settings, where adults may obtain substantial protection from disease, and children under 5 face the highest risk of death (Doolan et al., 2009; WHO Report 2020).
evidence: Cited from Doolan et al., 2009 and WHO Report 2020

claim: Children under 5 face the highest risk of death from malaria in endemic settings.
source: This naturally acquired immunity develops gradually with age and increasing cumulative exposure to P. falciparum in endemic settings, where adults may obtain substantial protection from disease, and children under 5 face the highest risk of death (Doolan et al., 2009; WHO Report 2020).
evidence: Cited from Doolan et al., 2009 and WHO Report 2020

claim: Antigenic variation, antigens containing repeat elements, and cross-reactive epitopes have been proposed to contribute to the slow development of immunity to malaria.
source: While a comprehensive understanding of the factors influencing the slow development of immunity is still lacking, certain properties of parasite antigens have been proposed to contribute (Portugal et al., 2013). These include, amongst other properties, antigenic variation, antigens containing repeat elements and cross-reactive epitopes (Anders, 1986; Reeder and Brown, 1996; Schofield, 1991).
evidence: Cited from Portugal et al., 2013; Anders, 1986; Reeder and Brown, 1996; Schofield, 1991

claim: Repeat elements are widely prevalent in the proteome of P. falciparum.
source: Repeat elements are widely prevalent in the proteome of P. falciparum and have been described to be highly immunogenic in a few antigens (Davies et al., 2017), such as the short, linear 'NANP' repeats from circumsporozoite protein (CSP) present in the RTS,S and R21 vaccines (Cockburn and Seder, 2018).
evidence: Cited from Davies et al., 2017

claim: The 'NANP' repeats from circumsporozoite protein (CSP) are present in the RTS,S and R21 vaccines.
source: Repeat elements are widely prevalent in the proteome of P. falciparum and have been described to be highly immunogenic in a few antigens (Davies et al., 2017), such as the short, linear 'NANP' repeats from circumsporozoite protein (CSP) present in the RTS,S and R21 vaccines (Cockburn and Seder, 2018).
evidence: Cited from Cockburn and Seder, 2018

claim: Increased valency of epitopes in repeat elements may lead to increased plasmablast formation by increasing the strength of the antigen-B-cell receptor interaction.
source: For instance, increased valency may lead to increased plasmablast formation by increasing the strength of the antigen-B-cell receptor (BCR) interaction, potentially altering the T-dependent response and inducing a T-independent response (Feldmann and Easten, 1971; Kato et al., 2020; O'Connor et al., 2006; Ochiai et al., 2013; Paus et al., 2006; Schofield, 1991; Schwickert et al., 2011).
evidence: Cited from multiple sources: Feldmann and Easten, 1971; Kato et al., 2020; O'Connor et al., 2006; Ochiai et al., 2013; Paus et al., 2006; Schofield, 1991; Schwickert et al., 2011

claim: Cross-reactive epitopes may negatively impact the affinity maturation process in malaria immunity.
source: A handful of cross-reactive epitopes have been reported in P. falciparum (Wåhlin et al., 1992) and have been proposed to negatively impact the affinity maturation process, although direct evidence is lacking (Anders, 1986).
evidence: Cited from Wåhlin et al., 1992 and Anders, 1986

claim: The Falciparome phage library contains 238,068 tiled 62-amino acid peptides covering all known coding regions of P. falciparum.
source: Towards this goal, we deployed a customized P. falciparum PhIP-seq T7 phage display library containing 238,068 tiled 62-amino acid peptides, covering all known coding regions, including antigenic variants, to systematically profile antibody targets in 198 Ugandan children and adults from high and moderate transmission settings.
evidence: Description of the library design used in the study

claim: The study profiled antibody targets in 198 Ugandan children and adults from high and moderate transmission settings.
source: Towards this goal, we deployed a customized P. falciparum PhIP-seq T7 phage display library containing 238,068 tiled 62-amino acid peptides, covering all known coding regions, including antigenic variants, to systematically profile antibody targets in 198 Ugandan children and adults from high and moderate transmission settings.
evidence: Description of study cohort

claim: Repeat elements were significantly enriched in antibody targets identified in the study.
source: Repeat elements – short amino acid sequences repeated within a protein – were significantly enriched in antibody targets.
evidence: Finding from the study's data analysis

claim: Breadth of responses to repeat-containing peptides was twofold higher in children living in the high versus moderate exposure setting.
source: While breadth of responses to repeat-containing peptides was twofold higher in children living in the high versus moderate exposure setting, no such differences were observed for peptides without repeats, suggesting that antibody responses to repeat-containing regions may be more exposure dependent and/or less durable in children than responses to regions without repeats.
evidence: Finding from the study's data analysis

claim: No differences in breadth of responses were observed between exposure settings for peptides without repeats.
source: While breadth of responses to repeat-containing peptides was twofold higher in children living in the high versus moderate exposure setting, no such differences were observed for peptides without repeats, suggesting that antibody responses to repeat-containing regions may be more exposure dependent and/or less durable in children than responses to regions without repeats.
evidence: Finding from the study's data analysis

claim: Antibody responses to repeat-containing regions may be more exposure dependent and/or less durable in children than responses to regions without repeats.
source: While breadth of responses to repeat-containing peptides was twofold higher in children living in the high versus moderate exposure setting, no such differences were observed for peptides without repeats, suggesting that antibody responses to repeat-containing regions may be more exposure dependent and/or less durable in children than responses to regions without repeats.
evidence: Interpretation of data findings

claim: Short motifs associated with seroreactivity were extensively shared among hundreds of antigens.
source: Additionally, short motifs associated with seroreactivity were extensively shared among hundreds of antigens, potentially representing cross-reactive epitopes.
evidence: Finding from the study's data analysis

claim: PfEMP1 shared motifs with the greatest number of other antigens.
source: PfEMP1 shared motifs with the greatest number of other antigens, partly driven by the diversity of PfEMP1 sequences.
evidence: Finding from the study's data analysis

claim: The diversity of PfEMP1 sequences partly drives the extensive motif sharing with other antigens.
source: PfEMP1 shared motifs with the greatest number of other antigens, partly driven by the diversity of PfEMP1 sequences.
evidence: Interpretation of data findings

claim: The large number of repeat elements and potential cross-reactive epitopes in P. falciparum could contribute to the inefficient nature of malaria immunity.
source: These data suggest that the large number of repeat elements and potential cross-reactive epitopes found within antigenic regions of P. falciparum could contribute to the inefficient nature of malaria immunity.
evidence: Interpretation and conclusion from study findings

claim: Tororo had very high malaria transmission at the time of sampling with an annual entomological inoculation rate of 49 infective bites per person.
source: For this study, we selected a single sample from each of 200 age-stratified individuals (children aged 2–11 years and adults) from two different sites in Uganda: Tororo, a region which had very high malaria transmission at the time of sampling (annual entomological inoculation rate [EIR] - 49 infective bites per person) and Kanungu, a region of moderately high transmission (EIR - 5 infective bites per person; Kamya et al., 2015).
evidence: Description of study site characteristics, cited from Kamya et al., 2015

claim: Kanungu had moderately high malaria transmission with an annual entomological inoculation rate of 5 infective bites per person.
source: For this study, we selected a single sample from each of 200 age-stratified individuals (children aged 2–11 years and adults) from two different sites in Uganda: Tororo, a region which had very high malaria transmission at the time of sampling (annual entomological inoculation rate [EIR] - 49 infective bites per person) and Kanungu, a region of moderately high transmission (EIR - 5 infective bites per person; Kamya et al., 2015).
evidence: Description of study site characteristics, cited from Kamya et al., 2015

claim: The majority of individuals from Tororo were positive for infection at the time of sampling.
source: While the majority of individuals from Tororo were positive for infection at the time of sampling, those from Kanungu were sampled at a median of 100 days after their previous infection.
evidence: Description of infection status in study cohort

claim: Individuals from Kanungu were sampled at a median of 100 days after their previous infection.
source: While the majority of individuals from Tororo were positive for infection at the time of sampling, those from Kanungu were sampled at a median of 100 days after their previous infection.
evidence: Description of infection status in study cohort

claim: Children acquire clinical immunity to malaria more rapidly in Tororo than Kanungu, consistent with higher rates of exposure.
source: We have previously shown that children acquire clinical immunity to malaria more rapidly in Tororo than Kanungu, consistent with higher rates of exposure (Rodriguez-Barraquer et al., 2018), and that adults at both sites have substantial immunity (Rek et al., 2016).
evidence: Cited from Rodriguez-Barraquer et al., 2018

claim: Adults at both Tororo and Kanungu sites have substantial immunity to malaria.
source: We have previously shown that children acquire clinical immunity to malaria more rapidly in Tororo than Kanungu, consistent with higher rates of exposure (Rodriguez-Barraquer et al., 2018), and that adults at both sites have substantial immunity (Rek et al., 2016).
evidence: Cited from Rek et al., 2016

claim: The Falciparome library includes peptides from 8980 protein sequences.
source: Overall, the library includes 238,068 peptides from 8980 protein sequences, including all known protein sequences from 2 reference strains (3D7 and IT) and extensive diversity of variant sequences from key antigens including PfEMP1s, RIFINs and STEVORs (Table 2, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Methods).
evidence: Description of library composition

claim: 223,145 peptides from 7577 proteins in the Falciparome library are from P. falciparum.
source: Of these, 223,145 peptides from 7577 proteins are from P. falciparum.
evidence: Description of library composition

claim: Greater than 99.5% of the programmed peptides were represented in the final packaged phage library.
source: Greater than 99.5% of the programmed peptides were represented in the final packaged phage library with relatively uniform distribution of abundance, with 90% of the peptides within a 16-fold difference (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Quality control data for the library

claim: 90% of the peptides in the Falciparome library were within a 16-fold difference in abundance.
source: Greater than 99.5% of the programmed peptides were represented in the final packaged phage library with relatively uniform distribution of abundance, with 90% of the peptides within a 16-fold difference (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Quality control data for the library shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: A total of 9927 peptides were identified as seroreactive across all samples.
source: Using this conservative approach, a total of 9927 peptides were identified as seroreactive across all samples, representing the identified targets of antibodies in this study (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Result from the filtering pipeline applied to the data

claim: The 9927 seroreactive peptides were derived from 1648 parasite proteins.
source: The 9927 seroreactive peptides identified by the pipeline were derived from 1648 parasite proteins ('seroreactive proteins') and antigenic variants, representing approximately 30% of the 5400 member proteome of P. falciparum, many of which showed broad seroreactivity across pediatric and adult Ugandan samples, whereas these same peptides showed no or rare seroreactivity in US controls (Figure 2a).
evidence: Result from the data analysis

claim: The seroreactive proteins represent approximately 30% of the 5400 member proteome of P. falciparum.
source: The 9927 seroreactive peptides identified by the pipeline were derived from 1648 parasite proteins ('seroreactive proteins') and antigenic variants, representing approximately 30% of the 5400 member proteome of P. falciparum, many of which showed broad seroreactivity across pediatric and adult Ugandan samples, whereas these same peptides showed no or rare seroreactivity in US controls (Figure 2a).
evidence: Calculation based on the number of seroreactive proteins identified

claim: The number of peptides enriched in children from moderate transmission settings was less than half of that in children in high transmission settings or adults in either setting.
source: The number of peptides enriched ('breadth') in children from moderate transmission settings was less than half of that in children in high transmission settings or adults in either setting (Figure 2b), an observation that we examined in greater detail below.
evidence: Result from the data analysis shown in Figure 2b

claim: The 1648 seroreactive proteins have reported expression across the lifecycle stages occurring in the human – sporozoite, asexual, and sexual blood stages.
source: The 1648 seroreactive proteins identified here have reported expression across the lifecycle stages occurring in the human – sporozoite, asexual, and sexual blood stages (Figure 2c).
evidence: Analysis of expression data shown in Figure 2c

claim: Among the 40 seroreactive proteins with the highest seropositivity, protective antibodies have been reported for 20 of them.
source: Among the 40 seroreactive proteins with the highest seropositivity (percent of people enriching for at least one seroreactive peptide in that protein), protective antibodies have been reported for 20 of them (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Analysis of literature on protective antibodies for identified proteins

claim: The top seroreactive proteins were enriched for those at the host-parasite interface.
source: Moreover, as expected, and consistent with previous studies, the top seroreactive proteins (Supplementary file 3) were enriched for those at the host-parasite interface (GO analysis – Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Gene ontology analysis of seroreactive proteins

claim: The proteins identified in this study overlapped substantially with antigenic proteins identified in previous protein array screens.
source: The proteins identified here overlapped substantially with antigenic proteins identified in previous protein array screens (28%, 49%, and 44% of those reported in Camponovo et al., 2020; Crompton et al., 2010; Helb et al., 2015 respectively).
evidence: Comparison with previous studies cited

claim: 952 proteins identified in this study were not identified in previous protein array studies.
source: However, this whole-proteome approach also identified 952 proteins not identified in the above studies.
evidence: Comparison with previous studies

claim: PhIP-seq detects predominantly linear epitopes, as opposed to conformational epitopes.
source: Antigens identified in previous studies may have not been enriched here because of a known limitation of PhIP-seq – it detects predominantly linear epitopes, as opposed to conformational epitopes, which would account for loss of sensitivity with respect to particular proteins.
evidence: Known limitation of the PhIP-seq method

claim: Breadth increased with age in both Tororo and Kanungu settings.
source: Breadth increased with age in both settings, occurring more rapidly in the higher transmission setting such that children reached a similar breadth as adults by age 11 (Figure 2b, Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Result from the data analysis shown in Figure 2b and Figure 2—figure supplement 5

claim: In the higher transmission setting, children reached a similar breadth as adults by age 11.
source: Breadth increased with age in both settings, occurring more rapidly in the higher transmission setting such that children reached a similar breadth as adults by age 11 (Figure 2b, Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Result from the data analysis shown in Figure 2b and Figure 2—figure supplement 5

claim: Children in the higher transmission setting had a significantly higher breadth than children in the moderate transmission setting.
source: As a result, children in the higher transmission setting had a significantly higher breadth than children in the moderate transmission setting.
evidence: Statistical comparison of breadth between settings

claim: Adults in both transmission settings had comparable breadth.
source: In contrast, adults in both settings had comparable breadth.
evidence: Statistical comparison of breadth between settings

claim: The Falciparome library includes 431 PfEMP1 members from seven strains.
source: Multiple variants from three VSA families were represented in the library - PfEMP1s (431 members from seven strains), RIFINs (157 3D7+118 IT), and STEVORs (32 3D7+32 IT variants), and the breadth of seroreactive variants was investigated across age and exposure based on the number of variant proteins in each family to which the VSA seroreactive peptides belonged in each person (Materials and methods; Figure 2d, Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Description of library composition

claim: The Falciparome library includes 157 3D7 and 118 IT RIFIN variants.
source: Multiple variants from three VSA families were represented in the library - PfEMP1s (431 members from seven strains), RIFINs (157 3D7+118 IT), and STEVORs (32 3D7+32 IT variants), and the breadth of seroreactive variants was investigated across age and exposure based on the number of variant proteins in each family to which the VSA seroreactive peptides belonged in each person (Materials and methods; Figure 2d, Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Description of library composition

claim: The Falciparome library includes 32 3D7 and 32 IT STEVOR variants.
source: Multiple variants from three VSA families were represented in the library - PfEMP1s (431 members from seven strains), RIFINs (157 3D7+118 IT), and STEVORs (32 3D7+32 IT variants), and the breadth of seroreactive variants was investigated across age and exposure based on the number of variant proteins in each family to which the VSA seroreactive peptides belonged in each person (Materials and methods; Figure 2d, Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Description of library composition

claim: In the moderate transmission setting, adults had a significantly higher breadth of PfEMP1 variants recognized than children.
source: In the moderate transmission setting, adults had a significantly higher breadth of PfEMP1 variants recognized than children (fold increase in median breadth in adults over 4–6 and 7–11 year-old children: 1.69; KS-test p-value <0.05), suggesting an age and/or cumulative exposure-dependent increase in PfEMP1 breadth in this setting, as previously observed in Cham et al., 2009.
evidence: Statistical analysis of VSA breadth data, cited from Cham et al., 2009

claim: The majority of seroreactivity in the moderate setting was present in the conserved ATS domain of PfEMP1, as opposed to the variable domains.
source: We note that the majority of seroreactivity in the moderate setting was present in the conserved ATS domain of PfEMP1, as opposed to the variable domains (Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Result from the data analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6

claim: Both children and adults in the moderate transmission setting poorly recognized RIFINs and STEVORs.
source: On the other hand, both children and adults in this setting poorly recognized RIFINs and STEVORs.
evidence: Result from the data analysis

claim: In the high transmission setting, children had a significantly higher breadth of variants recognized than adults for all three VSAs.
source: In contrast, in the high transmission setting, children had a significantly higher breadth of variants recognized than adults for all three VSAs.
evidence: Statistical analysis of VSA breadth data

claim: Children of 2–6 years in the high transmission setting had the broadest responses to RIFINs with a 17-fold increase in median breadth over adults.
source: Children of 2–6 years had the broadest responses to RIFINs (including in the variable V2 region) and STEVORS (fold increase in median breadth in 2- to 6-year-old children over adults for RIFINs: 17; KS-test p-value <0.05, for STEVORs: 21; KS-test p-value <0.05) and children of 4–11 years to PfEMP1s (including in the variable DBL domains; fold increase in median breadth in 4- to 11-year-old children over adults for PfEMP1: 2.13; KS-test p-value <0.05), suggesting a decline in responses to variants as children develop into adults in this setting.
evidence: Statistical analysis of VSA breadth data

claim: Children of 2–6 years in the high transmission setting had the broadest responses to STEVORs with a 21-fold increase in median breadth over adults.
source: Children of 2–6 years had the broadest responses to RIFINs (including in the variable V2 region) and STEVORS (fold increase in median breadth in 2- to 6-year-old children over adults for RIFINs: 17; KS-test p-value <0.05, for STEVORs: 21; KS-test p-value <0.05) and children of 4–11 years to PfEMP1s (including in the variable DBL domains; fold increase in median breadth in 4- to 11-year-old children over adults for PfEMP1: 2.13; KS-test p-value <0.05), suggesting a decline in responses to variants as children develop into adults in this setting.
evidence: Statistical analysis of VSA breadth data

claim: Children of 4–11 years in the high transmission setting had the broadest responses to PfEMP1s with a 2.13-fold increase in median breadth over adults.
source: Children of 2–6 years had the broadest responses to RIFINs (including in the variable V2 region) and STEVORS (fold increase in median breadth in 2- to 6-year-old children over adults for RIFINs: 17; KS-test p-value <0.05, for STEVORs: 21; KS-test p-value <0.05) and children of 4–11 years to PfEMP1s (including in the variable DBL domains; fold increase in median breadth in 4- to 11-year-old children over adults for PfEMP1: 2.13; KS-test p-value <0.05), suggesting a decline in responses to variants as children develop into adults in this setting.
evidence: Statistical analysis of VSA breadth data

claim: There is a decline in responses to VSA variants as children develop into adults in the high transmission setting.
source: Children of 2–6 years had the broadest responses to RIFINs (including in the variable V2 region) and STEVORS (fold increase in median breadth in 2- to 6-year-old children over adults for RIFINs: 17; KS-test p-value <0.05, for STEVORs: 21; KS-test p-value <0.05) and children of 4–11 years to PfEMP1s (including in the variable DBL domains; fold increase in median breadth in 4- to 11-year-old children over adults for PfEMP1: 2.13; KS-test p-value <0.05), suggesting a decline in responses to variants as children develop into adults in this setting.
evidence: Interpretation of VSA breadth data

claim: The decline in VSA breadth in adults in the high transmission setting is consistent with observations from a previous study investigating antibody responses to PfEMP1 DBLα domains in Papua New Guinea.
source: This is consistent with observations from a previous study investigating antibody responses to PfEMP1 DBLα domains in Papua New Guinea (Barry et al., 2011).
evidence: Cited from Barry et al., 2011

claim: The loss of VSA breadth in adults in the high transmission setting could be due to a decline in antibody levels to VSA variants due to reduced antigenic exposure.
source: The loss of VSA breadth in adults in the high transmission setting could be due to various reasons, including a decline in antibody levels to VSA variants due to reduced antigenic exposure, as adults have a lower parasitic load than children in this setting, or a shift in the focus of the immune response to less variable targets.
evidence: Speculation about possible mechanisms

claim: Adults have a lower parasitic load than children in the high transmission setting.
source: The loss of VSA breadth in adults in the high transmission setting could be due to various reasons, including a decline in antibody levels to VSA variants due to reduced antigenic exposure, as adults have a lower parasitic load than children in this setting, or a shift in the focus of the immune response to less variable targets.
evidence: Statement about parasitic load differences

claim: The loss of VSA breadth in adults could be due to a shift in the focus of the immune response to less variable targets.
source: The loss of VSA breadth in adults in the high transmission setting could be due to various reasons, including a decline in antibody levels to VSA variants due to reduced antigenic exposure, as adults have a lower parasitic load than children in this setting, or a shift in the focus of the immune response to less variable targets.
evidence: Speculation about possible mechanisms

claim: The decrease in VSA breadth in adults may reflect a transition from recognition of linear epitopes to conformational epitopes.
source: It may also be possible that the decrease in VSA breadth in adults reflects a transition from recognition of linear epitopes to conformational epitopes, which may not be detected in this assay (or prior microarray assays).
evidence: Speculation about possible mechanisms and assay limitations

claim: Seroreactive regions within FIRA, CSP, and LSA3 showed substantial overlap with a previous study using a high-density linear peptide array.
source: Comparison with a previous study using a high-density linear peptide array covering a subset of antigens showed substantial overlap of the seroreactive regions within these antigens (Jaenisch et al., 2019; Figure 3—figure supplement 1), although some differences were apparent.
evidence: Comparison with previous study cited from Jaenisch et al., 2019, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Differences in the length of peptides and nature of display may explain discrepancies between this study and previous peptide array studies.
source: Differences in the length of peptides as well as nature of display (linear 15-aa peptides on an array versus phage display of 62-aa peptides) are potential explanations for these discrepancies.
evidence: Speculation about methodological differences

claim: High-resolution maps of seroreactivity for over 1000 proteins were characterized for the first time in this dataset.
source: Importantly, high-resolution maps of seroreactivity for over 1000 proteins were characterized for the first time in our dataset (Figure 3b).
evidence: Description of novel findings in the study

claim: PHISTc has been previously described as an antigenic protein but not dissected at high resolution.
source: A notable example is, PHISTc (PF3D7_0801000), which has previously been described as an antigenic protein, but not dissected at high resolution (Baum et al., 2013; Dent et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from Baum et al., 2013 and Dent et al., 2015

claim: PHISTc is exported from the parasite during the asexual blood stage and has unknown function.
source: It is exported from the parasite during the asexual blood stage and has unknown function, although mildly protective antibodies have been described against the N-terminal segment (Nagaoka et al., 2021).
evidence: Cited from Nagaoka et al., 2021

claim: Mildly protective antibodies have been described against the N-terminal segment of PHISTc.
source: It is exported from the parasite during the asexual blood stage and has unknown function, although mildly protective antibodies have been described against the N-terminal segment (Nagaoka et al., 2021).
evidence: Cited from Nagaoka et al., 2021

claim: RON4 is part of the moving junction during merozoite invasion of the host.
source: Another example is RON4 (Rhoptry Neck Protein 4), part of the moving junction during merozoite invasion of the host (Morahan et al., 2009) and is also critical for sporozoite invasion of hepatocytes (Giovannini et al., 2011).
evidence: Cited from Morahan et al., 2009

claim: RON4 is critical for sporozoite invasion of hepatocytes.
source: Another example is RON4 (Rhoptry Neck Protein 4), part of the moving junction during merozoite invasion of the host (Morahan et al., 2009) and is also critical for sporozoite invasion of hepatocytes (Giovannini et al., 2011).
evidence: Cited from Giovannini et al., 2011

claim: Exposure-dependent seropositivity was observed at the B-cell epitope in CSP targeted by the RTS,S vaccine.
source: For instance, as expected (Kazmin et al., 2017), we observed exposure-dependent seropositivity at the B-cell epitope in CSP targeted by the RTS,S vaccine (NANP repeating sequence; Figure 3a).
evidence: Result from the data analysis shown in Figure 3a, cited from Kazmin et al., 2017

claim: The number of repeats in each protein sequence was significantly higher in the seroreactive proteins in comparison to non-seroreactive proteins.
source: The number of repeats in each protein sequence was significantly higher in the seroreactive proteins in comparison to non-seroreactive proteins (median number of repeats per protein: seroreactive proteins – 20; non-seroreactive proteins – 6; p-value = <0.001, based on 1000 iterations [1636 proteins per iteration] of random sampling of the non-seroreactive set; Figure 4a).
evidence: Statistical analysis of repeat frequency shown in Figure 4a

claim: The median number of repeats per protein is 20 for seroreactive proteins and 6 for non-seroreactive proteins.
source: The number of repeats in each protein sequence was significantly higher in the seroreactive proteins in comparison to non-seroreactive proteins (median number of repeats per protein: seroreactive proteins – 20; non-seroreactive proteins – 6; p-value = <0.001, based on 1000 iterations [1636 proteins per iteration] of random sampling of the non-seroreactive set; Figure 4a).
evidence: Statistical analysis of repeat frequency

claim: Seroreactive peptides yielded significantly higher repeat indices than non-seroreactive peptides from seroreactive proteins.
source: Overall, seroreactive peptides yielded significantly higher repeat indices than non-seroreactive peptides from seroreactive proteins, and this trend was more pronounced as a function of seropositivity (Figure 4c).
evidence: Statistical analysis of repeat indices shown in Figure 4c

claim: The median repeat index for non-seroreactive peptides was 1, while the median index for >10% and >40% seropositivity was 3 and 13 respectively, for a kmer of size 7.
source: The median repeat index for non-seroreactive peptides was 1, while the median index for >10% and>40% seropositivity was 3 and 13 respectively, for a kmer of size 7 (KS test p-value <0.05 between successive distributions).
evidence: Statistical analysis of repeat indices

claim: Seroreactive peptides are dominated by repeat elements and those with higher seropositivity have progressively higher repeat indices.
source: These results suggest that seroreactive peptides are dominated by repeat elements and those with higher seropositivity also have progressively higher repeat indices.
evidence: Interpretation of repeat index data

claim: The relationship between seropositivity and repeat index was consistently observed regardless of kmer size from 6 to 9aa.
source: This relationship was consistently observed, regardless of kmer size from 6 to 9aa, and was insensitive to the level of degeneracy or biochemical similarity used for determining repeat matches (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Robustness analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: Seroreactive proteins tend to be repeat-containing proteins.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that seroreactive proteins tend to be repeat-containing proteins, and within these proteins, the individual seroreactive peptides tend to be those that contain the repeats.
evidence: Summary interpretation of repeat analysis data

claim: Within seroreactive proteins, the individual seroreactive peptides tend to be those that contain the repeats.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that seroreactive proteins tend to be repeat-containing proteins, and within these proteins, the individual seroreactive peptides tend to be those that contain the repeats.
evidence: Summary interpretation of repeat analysis data

claim: Seroreactive regions that are shared widely among individuals tend to feature higher numbers of repeat elements.
source: Furthermore, seroreactive regions that are shared widely among individuals tend to feature higher numbers of repeat elements.
evidence: Summary interpretation of repeat analysis data

claim: For non-repeat containing peptides, breadth was significantly higher in adults than children in both exposure settings.
source: For the set of non-repeat containing peptides, breadth (number of non-repeat peptides enriched per person) was significantly higher in adults than children in both exposure settings (percent increase in median breadth in adults over 4- to 6-year old children: moderate setting – 28%; high setting – 20%; Figure 5a).
evidence: Statistical analysis of breadth shown in Figure 5a

claim: For non-repeat containing peptides, there was no significant difference in breadth between the two exposure settings within each age group.
source: However, within each set of age groups, there was no significant difference in breadth between the two exposure settings.
evidence: Statistical analysis of breadth

claim: For repeat-containing seroreactive peptides, breadth was higher in adults than children in both exposure settings.
source: Similar to non-repeat peptides, breadth of these peptides was higher in adults than children, reaching a similar level in both exposure settings (percent increase in median breadth in adults over 4- to 6-year-old children: moderate setting – 193%; high setting – 56%).
evidence: Statistical analysis of breadth

claim: Children living in the high versus moderate exposure setting had twice the breadth of repeat-containing peptides.
source: In contrast to non-repeat peptides however, there was an exposure dependence in the responses to repeat-containing peptides with age, such that children living in the high versus moderate exposure setting had twice the breadth of repeat-containing peptides, reaching the same level in adulthood in both settings (Figure 5b).
evidence: Statistical analysis of breadth shown in Figure 5b

claim: Individual repeat elements showed higher seropositivity in the high exposure setting compared to moderate exposure in children, but not adults.
source: Investigation of individual repeat elements recapitulated this trend and showed higher seropositivity in the high exposure setting compared to moderate exposure in children, but not adults (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Analysis of individual repeat elements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2

claim: Repeat elements from PHISTc, LSA3, and FIRA did not show a transmission setting-dependent response in children.
source: There were a small number of notable exceptions, including repeat elements from PHISTc (PF3D7_0801000), LSA3 (PF3D7_0220000), and FIRA (PF3D7_0501400), none of which showed a transmission setting-dependent response in children (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Analysis of individual repeat elements

claim: In the moderate exposure setting, the median number of days since last infection was 100.
source: In the moderate exposure setting, the median number of days since last infection was 100, whereas over 65% of the samples from the high exposure setting were taken during periods of active infection.
evidence: Description of cohort characteristics

claim: Over 65% of the samples from the high exposure setting were taken during periods of active infection.
source: In the moderate exposure setting, the median number of days since last infection was 100, whereas over 65% of the samples from the high exposure setting were taken during periods of active infection.
evidence: Description of cohort characteristics

claim: For repeat containing peptides, breadth was significantly increased in the high exposure setting relative to moderate exposure, regardless of infection status at the time of sampling.
source: For repeat containing peptides, breadth was significantly increased in the high exposure setting relative to moderate exposure, regardless of infection status at the time of sampling.
evidence: Statistical analysis controlling for infection status

claim: The difference in breadth between exposure settings was not observed for non-repeat containing peptides when controlling for infection status.
source: This difference was not observed for non-repeat containing peptides (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Statistical analysis controlling for infection status shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3

claim: The data suggest a dependency on cumulative exposure for the observed differential antibody responses in children to repeat-containing peptides relative to non-repeat peptides.
source: These data suggest a dependency on cumulative exposure for the observed differential antibody responses in children to repeat-containing peptides relative to non-repeat peptides.
evidence: Interpretation of data controlling for infection status

claim: For repeat containing peptides, a significant decrease in breadth was evident between the most recent infections (0–30 days) and the longest (240–360 days) in the moderate exposure setting.
source: For repeat containing peptides, a significant decrease in breadth was evident between the most recent infections (0–30 days) and the longest (240–360 days) in the moderate exposure setting, while the difference in the high exposure setting between 0–30 days and 60–120 days was not significant; notably everyone in this setting was infected within the prior 120 days.
evidence: Statistical analysis of breadth over time since infection

claim: No significant difference in breadth over time since infection was evident for non-repeat peptides in either setting.
source: No significant difference was evident for non-repeat peptides in either setting.
evidence: Statistical analysis of breadth over time since infection

claim: The results are consistent with the notion that the antibody response to repeat containing peptides are short lived relative to non-repeat peptides.
source: Together, these results are consistent with the notion that the antibody response to repeat containing peptides are short lived relative to non-repeat peptides.
evidence: Interpretation of durability analysis data

claim: Antibody responses to repeat-containing peptides may be less efficiently acquired and/or maintained in children than non-repeat peptides, but plateau at the same level of prevalence in adulthood.
source: Overall, the above data show that antibody responses to repeat-containing peptides may be less efficiently acquired and/or maintained in children than non-repeat peptides, but plateau at the same level of prevalence in adulthood.
evidence: Summary interpretation of repeat peptide response data

claim: A total of 911 significantly enriched inter-protein motifs were identified using a kmer size of 7 and allowing for up to two biochemically conservative substitutions.
source: Using a kmer size of 7, and allowing for up to two biochemically conservative substitutions, a total of 911 significantly enriched inter-protein motifs were identified, representing 509 seroreactive proteins (Supplementary file 6).
evidence: Result from inter-protein motif analysis

claim: The 911 inter-protein motifs represent 509 seroreactive proteins.
source: Using a kmer size of 7, and allowing for up to two biochemically conservative substitutions, a total of 911 significantly enriched inter-protein motifs were identified, representing 509 seroreactive proteins (Supplementary file 6).
evidence: Result from inter-protein motif analysis

claim: The inter-protein motifs had a lower hydrophobicity index (mean Kyle-Doolittle=–1.95) than a random set of motifs in the proteome.
source: Taken as a group, the collected motifs had a lower hydrophobicity index (mean Kyle-Doolittle=–1.95), a lower net charge (mean = –0.47; at pH 7), enrichment of charged glutamate, lysine, asparagine, and aspartate residues and depletion of cysteine and hydrophobic residues than a random set of motifs in the proteome (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Biochemical characterization of inter-protein motifs shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: The inter-protein motifs had a lower net charge (mean = –0.47 at pH 7) than a random set of motifs in the proteome.
source: Taken as a group, the collected motifs had a lower hydrophobicity index (mean Kyle-Doolittle=–1.95), a lower net charge (mean = –0.47; at pH 7), enrichment of charged glutamate, lysine, asparagine, and aspartate residues and depletion of cysteine and hydrophobic residues than a random set of motifs in the proteome (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Biochemical characterization of inter-protein motifs shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: The inter-protein motifs showed enrichment of charged glutamate, lysine, asparagine, and aspartate residues and depletion of cysteine and hydrophobic residues compared to random motifs.
source: Taken as a group, the collected motifs had a lower hydrophobicity index (mean Kyle-Doolittle=–1.95), a lower net charge (mean = –0.47; at pH 7), enrichment of charged glutamate, lysine, asparagine, and aspartate residues and depletion of cysteine and hydrophobic residues than a random set of motifs in the proteome (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Biochemical characterization of inter-protein motifs shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: The biochemical characteristics of inter-protein motifs are consistent with those observed in prior studies of residues in B cell epitopes.
source: These biochemical characteristics are consistent with those observed in prior studies of residues in B cell epitopes (Akbar et al., 2021; Rubinstein et al., 2008).
evidence: Cited from Akbar et al., 2021 and Rubinstein et al., 2008

claim: The maximum seropositivity among peptides containing an inter-protein motif was on average 54-fold higher than the maximum seropositivity among overlapping peptides not containing the motif.
source: The maximum seropositivity among peptides containing an inter-protein motif was on average 54-fold higher than the maximum seropositivity among overlapping peptides not containing the motif (using a pseudo-seropositivity of 0.1% for peptides with 0% seropositivity to facilitate fold change calculation), suggesting a strong association between seroreactivity and the inter-protein motif itself, not just the whole peptide within which it resides (comparison of median seropositivity yielded a similar result).
evidence: Analysis of overlapping peptides to localize seroreactivity

claim: There is a strong association between seroreactivity and the inter-protein motif itself, not just the whole peptide within which it resides.
source: The maximum seropositivity among peptides containing an inter-protein motif was on average 54-fold higher than the maximum seropositivity among overlapping peptides not containing the motif (using a pseudo-seropositivity of 0.1% for peptides with 0% seropositivity to facilitate fold change calculation), suggesting a strong association between seroreactivity and the inter-protein motif itself, not just the whole peptide within which it resides (comparison of median seropositivity yielded a similar result).
evidence: Interpretation of overlapping peptide analysis

claim: Shared seroreactivity of inter-protein motifs within individuals was significantly higher than in randomly drawn peptides lacking these motifs.
source: We observed that shared seroreactivity of inter-protein motifs within individuals was significantly higher than in the randomly drawn peptides lacking these motifs (KS test p-value <0.01).
evidence: Statistical analysis of co-occurrence of reactivity

claim: The data suggest a possibility for cross-reactivity to inter-protein motifs within individuals.
source: Overall, these data suggest a possibility for cross-reactivity to these motifs within individuals.
evidence: Interpretation of co-occurrence analysis

claim: The data on inter-protein motifs were derived from complex polyclonal responses in each person, and do not represent direct evaluation of the cross-reactivity of single antibodies.
source: However, it is important to note that these data were derived from complex polyclonal responses in each person, and do not represent direct evaluation of the cross-reactivity of single antibodies.
evidence: Limitation of the cross-reactivity analysis

claim: On average, each inter-protein motif was shared by 3 seroreactive proteins (median = 2).
source: On average, each inter-protein motif was shared by 3 seroreactive proteins (median = 2).
evidence: Summary statistic of motif sharing

claim: Among the 509 seroreactive proteins, each of them shared inter-protein motifs with six other proteins on average (median = 3).
source: Among the 509 seroreactive proteins, each of them shared inter-protein motifs with six other proteins on average (median = 3), (Supplementary file 8, Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Summary statistic of motif sharing

claim: The PfEMP1 family possessed at least 90 shared inter-protein motifs.
source: The PfEMP1 family of proteins possessed at least 90 shared inter-protein motifs, and this family shared those motifs with the greatest number of other seroreactive proteins (57) compared to all other proteins in this analysis.
evidence: Analysis of PfEMP1 motif sharing

claim: The PfEMP1 family shared motifs with 57 other seroreactive proteins.
source: The PfEMP1 family of proteins possessed at least 90 shared inter-protein motifs, and this family shared those motifs with the greatest number of other seroreactive proteins (57) compared to all other proteins in this analysis.
evidence: Analysis of PfEMP1 motif sharing

claim: Approximately five times as many proteins shared connections with PfEMP1 than would be expected by chance.
source: Approximately five times as many proteins shared connections with PfEMP1 than would be expected by chance (PfEMP1 shared motifs with 12–16 other proteins using a set of 9927 peptides consisting of PfEMP1 seroreactive peptides + random non-PfEMP1 peptides).
evidence: Statistical comparison with random expectation

claim: The extent of motif sharing by PfEMP1 was driven, in part, by the number of PfEMP1 sequences included in the analysis.
source: This extent of sharing was driven, in part, by the number of PfEMP1 sequences included in the analysis.
evidence: Interpretation of PfEMP1 motif sharing analysis

claim: When using PfEMP1 peptides from only PF3D7 and PFIT genomes instead of 7 genomes, PfEMP1 shared motifs with 32 seroreactive proteins instead of 57.
source: This was apparent when the same analysis performed with a reduced diversity of PfEMP1 sequences in the seroreactive peptide set (using PfEMP1 peptides from only PF3D7 and PFIT genomes instead of 7 genomes) resulted in PfEMP1 sharing motifs with 32 seroreactive proteins instead of 57.
evidence: Analysis with reduced PfEMP1 diversity

claim: The extent of motif sharing for PfEMP1 observed in this study may only be a small fraction of that occurring in the extensive natural diversity of PfEMP1 variants in circulating parasites.
source: This suggests that the extent of sharing for PfEMP1 observed in this study may only be a small fraction of that occurring in the extensive natural diversity of PfEMP1 variants in circulating parasites.
evidence: Interpretation and extrapolation from reduced diversity analysis

claim: 495 seroreactive proteins outside the main PfEMP1 network were highly connected to each other through motif sharing.
source: Outside the main network driven by PfEMP1, 495 seroreactive proteins were also found to be highly connected to each other through motif sharing (Figure 6—figure supplement 5a).
evidence: Network analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 5a

claim: A large proportion of proteins with high seropositivity were connected through motif sharing (80% and 58% of proteins with >30% and 10–30% seropositivity, respectively).
source: A large proportion of proteins with high seropositivity were connected (80% and 58% of proteins with >30% and 10–30% seropositivity, respectively).
evidence: Analysis of connectivity among high seropositivity proteins

claim: 80% of proteins in the motif-sharing network had reported expression in the asexual blood stage of the lifecycle of P. falciparum.
source: Moreover, 80% of proteins in this network had reported expression in the asexual blood stage of the lifecycle of P. falciparum (PlasmoDB), suggesting temporally concordant presence of proteins sharing motifs within their seroreactive regions.
evidence: Analysis of expression data from PlasmoDB

claim: The inter-protein motifs are strongly associated with seroreactivity.
source: These results indicate that the interprotein motifs are strongly associated with seroreactivity and are extensively shared across seroreactive proteins, including among regions highly targeted by the antibodies.
evidence: Summary interpretation of inter-protein motif analysis

claim: Inter-protein motifs are extensively shared across seroreactive proteins, including among regions highly targeted by the antibodies.
source: These results indicate that the interprotein motifs are strongly associated with seroreactivity and are extensively shared across seroreactive proteins, including among regions highly targeted by the antibodies.
evidence: Summary interpretation of inter-protein motif analysis

claim: PhIP-seq for P. falciparum offers several attractive advantages including coverage of >99.5% of the proteome.
source: The library described here contains >99.5% of the proteome, including variants for several antigenic families, surpassing the coverage of other existing proteome-wide tools for P. falciparum (Camponovo et al., 2020; Morita et al., 2017), while simultaneously providing high-resolution characterization of antigens (up to 12–13 aa regions within peptides).
evidence: Comparison with other methods cited from Camponovo et al., 2020 and Morita et al., 2017

claim: The Falciparome library provides high-resolution characterization of antigens up to 12–13 aa regions within peptides.
source: The library described here contains >99.5% of the proteome, including variants for several antigenic families, surpassing the coverage of other existing proteome-wide tools for P. falciparum (Camponovo et al., 2020; Morita et al., 2017), while simultaneously providing high-resolution characterization of antigens (up to 12–13 aa regions within peptides).
evidence: Description of library resolution capability

claim: The PhIP-seq platform converts a proteomic assay into a genomic assay, leveraging the massive scale and low-cost nature of next-generation short-read sequencing.
source: Unlike peptide arrays, the platform converts a proteomic assay into a genomic assay, leveraging the massive scale and low-cost nature of next-generation short-read sequencing.
evidence: Description of platform advantages

claim: The PhIP-seq platform is cost-effective and scalable, allowing for the processing of hundreds of samples in parallel.
source: The result is a cost-effective and scalable system, allowing for the processing of hundreds of samples in parallel.
evidence: Description of platform advantages

claim: Phage display systems have the ability to sequentially enrich, release phage, and repeat, greatly amplifying the signal to noise.
source: Finally, an important aspect of all phage display systems is the ability to sequentially enrich, release phage, and repeat, thus greatly amplifying the signal to noise (O'Donovan et al., 2020; Smith and Petrenko, 1997).
evidence: Cited from O'Donovan et al., 2020 and Smith and Petrenko, 1997

claim: The high immunogenicity of repeat sequences may be the result of competitive advantages that B cell clones encounter when binding to higher valency epitopes.
source: The high immunogenicity of repeat sequences observed here may be the result of competitive advantages that B cell clones could encounter when binding to higher valency epitopes, as opposed to single copy epitopes.
evidence: Speculation about mechanism of repeat immunogenicity

claim: Evidence from experimental inoculations of antigens with differing repeat numbers supports the notion that B cell clones have competitive advantages when binding to higher valency epitopes.
source: Evidence from experimental inoculations of antigens with differing repeat numbers support this notion (Kato et al., 2020).
evidence: Cited from Kato et al., 2020

claim: Tandem repeat regions are predicted to be intrinsically disordered, which in turn have favorable predictions as linear B cell epitopes.
source: Moreover, tandem repeat regions are predicted to be intrinsically disordered, which in turn have favorable predictions as linear B cell epitopes (Guy et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from Guy et al., 2015

claim: High immunogenicity of repeat elements can potentially restrict responses to other epitopes within the antigen.
source: Notably, this high immunogenicity can potentially restrict responses to other epitopes within the antigen, as has been reported for responses to protective non-repeat epitopes in the circumsporozoite protein (CSP; Chatterjee et al., 2021).
evidence: Cited from Chatterjee et al., 2021

claim: The predominance of repeat containing peptides in antibody targets, along with the abundance of these peptides in the P. falciparum proteome, suggests a possible strategy evolved by the parasite for diverting the humoral response towards short-lived or exposure-dependent responses.
source: Regardless, the predominance of repeat containing peptides in antibody targets, along with the remarkable abundance of these peptides in the P. falciparum proteome, suggests a possible strategy evolved by the parasite for the purpose of diverting the humoral response towards short-lived or exposure-dependent responses.
evidence: Interpretation and speculation about evolutionary strategy

claim: The hypothesis of less durable antibody responses to repeat antigens in P. falciparum can be reconciled with a model in which repeating epitopes favor extrafollicular B cell responses, which are typically short-lived.
source: The hypothesis of less durable antibody responses to repeat antigens in P. falciparum can be reconciled with a model in which repeating epitopes favor extrafollicular B cell responses, which are typically short-lived (Cockburn and Seder, 2018; Schofield, 1991).
evidence: Cited from Cockburn and Seder, 2018 and Schofield, 1991

claim: Strong binding of BCR to the antigen, including through increased valency, increases the production of plasmablasts.
source: Several studies provide support to this model, where strong binding of BCR to the antigen, including through increased valency, increases the production of plasmablasts (Kato et al., 2020; O'Connor et al., 2006; Ochiai et al., 2013; Paus et al., 2006; Schwickert et al., 2011).
evidence: Cited from multiple sources: Kato et al., 2020; O'Connor et al., 2006; Ochiai et al., 2013; Paus et al., 2006; Schwickert et al., 2011

claim: Some studies have reported a decrease in long-lived plasma cells following increased strength of BCR-antigen interaction.
source: More insights come from a few studies that measured the outcome of GCs following increased strength of BCR-antigen interaction and these have reported a decrease in LLPCs (Fink et al., 2007) and IgG-switched memory cells (Pape et al., 2018; Taylor et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from Fink et al., 2007; Pape et al., 2018; Taylor et al., 2015

claim: Extensive presence of potential cross-reactive epitopes in P. falciparum antigens may play an important role in influencing the quality of the immune response to malaria.
source: Extensive presence of potential cross-reactive epitopes in P. falciparum antigens may play an important role in influencing the quality of the immune response to malaria.
evidence: Interpretation of cross-reactive epitope findings

claim: Simultaneous presence of cross-reactive epitopes could frustrate the affinity maturation process due to conflicting selection forces, as was observed for variant HIV antigens.
source: While it could be advantageous for the host if multiple parasite proteins could be targeted by antibodies through cross-reactivity, simultaneous presence of cross-reactive epitopes could alternatively frustrate the affinity maturation process due to conflicting selection forces, as was observed for variant HIV antigens (Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from Wang et al., 2015

claim: Recurrent exposure may be necessary for the generation of strong cross-binding antibodies to cross-reactive epitopes.
source: Further, recurrent exposure may be necessary for the generation of strong cross-binding antibodies to cross-reactive epitopes (Murugan et al., 2020).
evidence: Cited from Murugan et al., 2020

claim: The extensive presence of cross-reactive epitopes in P. falciparum may represent an evolutionary strategy aimed at limiting high-affinity antibodies in favor of lower affinity, cross reactive antibodies.
source: Thus, the extensive presence of cross-reactive epitopes, both within and between antigenic proteins in P. falciparum, could represent an evolutionary strategy aimed at limiting high-affinity antibodies in favor of lower affinity, cross reactive antibodies.
evidence: Speculation about evolutionary strategy

claim: The large number of shared seroreactive sequences in P. falciparum may represent a complex immune counter measure, resulting in inefficient immunity acquisition which requires extensive exposure.
source: In essence, the large number of shared seroreactive sequences in P. falciparum may represent a complex immune counter measure, resulting in inefficient immunity acquisition which requires extensive exposure.
evidence: Interpretation and speculation about immune evasion strategy

claim: As one becomes naturally exposed to different PfEMP1 variants, there may be an increase in not only the sequence diversity, but the number of cross-reactive epitopes that the immune system encounters.
source: This was driven in part by the wide diversity of PfEMP1 variants, indicating that as one becomes naturally exposed to different PfEMP1 variants (Cham et al., 2009), there may be an increase in not only the sequence diversity, but the number of cross-reactive epitopes that the immune system encounters.
evidence: Interpretation of PfEMP1 motif sharing data, cited from Cham et al., 2009

claim: Possessing cross-reactive epitopes with other antigens could result in binding of pre-existing antibodies to new PfEMP1 variants, which could be disadvantageous to the host if binding strength is weak.
source: Possessing cross-reactive epitopes with other antigens could result in binding of pre-existing antibodies to the new variants, which could be disadvantageous to the host if binding strength is weak.
evidence: Speculation about consequences of cross-reactivity

claim: Cross-reactivity may inhibit generation of antibodies specific to new PfEMP1 variants due to original antigenic sin.
source: Further, cross-reactivity may inhibit generation of antibodies specific to the new variant due to original antigenic sin (Vatti et al., 2017).
evidence: Cited from Vatti et al., 2017

claim: The mechanism of evolving PfEMP1 variants within a network of shared sequences with other antigens could be another strategy evolved by the parasite for immune evasion.
source: Thus, the mechanism of evolving PfEMP1 variants within a network of shared sequences with other antigens could be another strategy evolved by the parasite for immune evasion.
evidence: Speculation about evolutionary strategy

claim: Binding of new PfEMP1 variants to pre-existing antibodies may be advantageous to the host if those antibodies are effective against the new variants.
source: On the other hand, binding of new variants to pre-existing antibodies may be advantageous to the host if those antibodies are effective against the new variants.
evidence: Speculation about potential advantages of cross-reactivity

claim: Phage display of small peptides may not capture antibodies binding to conformational epitopes.
source: While phage display of small peptides yields high-resolution discrimination of linear epitopes, this approach may not capture antibodies binding to conformational epitopes.
evidence: Known limitation of the method

claim: The bias towards linear epitopes may have increased the relative detectability of repeat regions by the PhIP-seq assay.
source: The bias towards linear epitopes may have increased the relative detectability of repeat regions by this assay since they often form intrinsically disordered regions.
evidence: Speculation about potential bias in the assay

claim: Antibodies that depend on epitopes with disulfide linkages and post-translational modifications for binding would likely not be enriched using phage-presented peptides.
source: Furthermore, antibodies that depend on epitopes with disulfide linkages and post-translational modifications for binding would likely not be enriched using phage-presented peptides.
evidence: Known limitation of the method

claim: The PhIP-seq technique does not inherently provide quantitative measures of antibody affinity or titer.
source: Another limitation of our study is that the PhIP-seq technique does not inherently provide quantitative measures of antibody affinity or titer, as many factors influence the actual number of reads recovered after immunoprecipitation, such as starting copy number in the library and non-specific interactions with beads.
evidence: Known limitation of the method

claim: The analysis relies on per peptide relative enrichments, using non-malaria control sera as the basis for comparison.
source: Instead, our analysis relies on per peptide relative (ratiometric) enrichments, using non-malaria control (n=86) sera as the basis for comparison, which also serves to remove non-specific enrichments.
evidence: Description of analytical approach

claim: A stringent filter was imposed requiring that each seroreactive peptide be enriched in at least five Ugandan samples over control sera.
source: We imposed a stringent filter to minimize false positives by requiring that each seroreactive peptide be enriched in at least five Ugandan samples over control sera.
evidence: Description of filtering approach

claim: The stringent filter excluded possible seroreactive peptides unique to a single sample, but enriched for seroreactive peptides that represent common serological responses to malaria.
source: While this excluded possible seroreactive peptides unique to a single sample, the resulting sequences that passed were those that exhibited a minimum level of sharing among multiple individuals, thereby enriching for those seroreactive peptides that represent common serological responses to malaria.
evidence: Justification for filtering approach

claim: In natural infections in children, repeat regions in P. falciparum could lead to an exposure-dependent and/or short-lived antibody response to a higher degree than for non-repeat regions.
source: Results from our study suggest that that in natural infections in children, repeat regions in P. falciparum could lead to an exposure-dependent and/or short-lived antibody response to a higher degree than for non-repeat regions.
evidence: Summary of study findings

claim: Vaccine induced immunity is distinct from naturally acquired immunity.
source: While we recognize that vaccine induced immunity is distinct from naturally acquired immunity, this potential limitation should be considered when evaluating repeat-containing antigens as vaccine targets.
evidence: Acknowledgment of difference between vaccine and natural immunity

claim: The potential limitation of repeat-containing antigens should be considered when evaluating them as vaccine targets.
source: While we recognize that vaccine induced immunity is distinct from naturally acquired immunity, this potential limitation should be considered when evaluating repeat-containing antigens as vaccine targets.
evidence: Recommendation based on study findings

claim: Highly immunogenic regions in natural immunity to malaria are predominantly repeats.
source: Further, given that highly immunogenic regions in natural immunity to malaria are predominantly repeats and there is widespread presence of potential cross-reactive epitopes across many proteins, whole-parasite vaccines may also be susceptible to similar limitations.
evidence: Summary of study findings

claim: Whole-parasite vaccines may be susceptible to limitations due to repeat elements and cross-reactive epitopes.
source: Further, given that highly immunogenic regions in natural immunity to malaria are predominantly repeats and there is widespread presence of potential cross-reactive epitopes across many proteins, whole-parasite vaccines may also be susceptible to similar limitations.
evidence: Speculation based on study findings

claim: If the findings from this study translate to vaccine-induced immune responses, non-repetitive, unique antigenic regions may be more effective targets.
source: If the findings from this study translate to vaccine-induce immune responses, non-repetitive, unique antigenic regions may be more effective targets.
evidence: Recommendation based on study findings
